docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text: The questions I get asked, or should be asked, with the short answer. The detail is in each decision page.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In one sentence, what is Taloslab?

A complete Kubernetes platform that I operate solo on Hetzner for €41/month. A developer fills in a Backstage form, and their application is online with its database, DNS, TLS, secrets and monitoring, entirely through GitOps.

Why build all this for a single user?

To practice the platform engineer job on a real system, not on a tutorial. Every choice has a real cost in euros, and every outage has to be fixed by me. The single-user constraint is deliberate: it explains several choices, such as the absence of high availability or Kyverno in audit mode, and I can say what would change with a team.

What would you do differently?

On managed Kubernetes, measure etcd latency from day one, before migrating the GitOps. And isolate earlier the components that instrument other processes: an eBPF probe can mimic the bug of another tool.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
Why Talos rather than Ubuntu + kubeadm?

Talos is immutable, with no SSH or shell, driven by API. There is nothing to patch by hand and no configuration drift, and the attack surface is minimal. The cluster is recreated often: a declarative OS suits that better.

Why not managed Kubernetes?

I tried two. Infomaniak had recurring API timeouts; Scaleway, 0.73 s per etcd request on its shared control plane. I came back to Hetzner, where I control the network, Cilium with Gateway API included. → 004

A single control plane, isn't that risky?

It is: etcd has no fault tolerance. But three control planes triple the most expensive line item, for a service with no third-party users. In exchange: a daily etcd snapshot outside Hetzner and a full rebuild through Terraform + GitOps. → 002

How did you choose the machine size?

By measurement. On 2 vCPU, the control plane hit 132% CPU during the initial sync, with no memory alert: the controllers restarted in a chain. On 4 vCPU, it drops to 28%, for €3.60 more per month.

docs.title: GitOps
docs.text:
Why ArgoCD? You had moved to Flux.

I tested Flux for four months, when Flux Operator's Web UI came out. Its architecture is better, but it is harder to pick up, and ArgoCD remains the market standard. The outage that had accelerated the move actually came from eBPF instrumentation: I verified it with an A/B (334 git fetch, 0 errors) before switching back. → 005

How do you handle deployment order without dependsOn?

Waves: the next wave waits until the whole previous one is synced and healthy. ArgoCD disables health for child Applications by default, so I re-enable it with a Lua script, without which the waves wait for nothing. → 006

Tell me about an incident.

During a migration of the GitOps repo, ArgoCD applied the old definition of an Application to the new files and triggered a deletion. Defense in depth worked: the Kyverno policy blocked the cascade, and the database was restored to the second from the archived logs, with no data loss. Since then, this type of change is made in two commits, and a CI check prevents the cause from coming back. → Incident

Why not the Rendered Manifests Pattern?

ArgoCD's native implementation cannot express 23 of my 37 Applications. Rendered in CI, the result diverges from the cluster for 17 charts out of 22. A render diff posted as a comment on each PR gives me the same review with no artifact to maintain. → 012

docs.title: Platform
docs.text:
Why Crossplane rather than a shared Helm chart?

Crossplane reconciles continuously and exposes a readable status, and the developer only sees a 15-line API instead of all of a chart's values. The logic is in Python, tested end to end on Kind in CI. → 007

Where are the secrets?

In Infisical. External Secrets syncs them into the cluster, and Reloader restarts the pods on rotation. There is nothing in Git, and nothing in the Terraform state thanks to write-only attributes. → 009

Kyverno in audit mode, isn't that a bit light?

For best practices, yes, and it is deliberate: a single person deploys. The only blocking rule protects what cannot be rebuilt, the data, and it has already proven useful in an incident. With a team, I would switch to enforcement rule by rule. → 010

How is observability organized?

The Victoria stack (metrics, logs, traces) with Grafana and Slack alerts, plus Gatus for availability as seen from outside. The application is instrumented with the OpenTelemetry SDK, after the removal of an eBPF instrumentation that was corrupting processes. → 011

docs.title: SRE agent
docs.text:
You let an LLM modify your production?

No. The agent, still in development, runs in manual mode: it investigates and proposes, a human decides, and a GitOps-managed resource is only fixed through a pull request. An automatic mode will only come after tool-by-tool least-privilege hardening. → sre-agent

Why not use kagent or an LLM gateway?

A shared platform only pays off with several consumers, and there is only one. kagent would replace deterministic, tested code with prompting. I would re-evaluate it behind a reliability test, once several agents are in place.

docs.title: Lessons learned
docs.text: Outages are the most instructive part of the project. Each one follows the same format: symptom → cause → fix → lesson.

docs.title: A GitOps migration that triggered a deletion, restored with no loss
docs.text:
Context. While removing Kustomize from the GitOps repo, ArgoCD deleted (pruned) the resources of two applications, including their PostgreSQL database.

Cause. Between the merge of a commit and the application of an Application's new definition, ArgoCD runs the old definition against the new files. The old one could only read the folder through its Kustomize file, which had just been deleted. ArgoCD read the folder in non-recursive mode, found almost nothing, and removed the rest. The prune: false added in the same commit could not protect anything: it only took effect with the new definition.

What worked.

  • Guardrail: the Kyverno policy that protects data refused the deletion of the Crossplane resources and stopped the cascade.
  • Restore: point-in-time recovery (PITR) from the PostgreSQL logs continuously archived to B2, using the scripted procedure already exercised during cluster rebuilds. No data loss: the archive chain covered up to six seconds after the deletion began.

What I changed afterwards.

  1. A change that touches both a definition and the content it reads is made in two commits: first the definition, verified on the cluster, then the content.
  2. A CI check now verifies that every Application explicitly declares its read mode, and forbids Kustomize files from coming back.
  3. A migration is judged on pod creation time, not only on Healthy / Synced.

What it shows. A protection written in the commit that creates the risk does not cover that commit, and a render diff in CI cannot see the transition window, since it compares final states. Defense in depth (admission guardrail + continuous backup + rehearsed restore) did its job.

docs.title: A "Healthy" component rendered with its default values
docs.text:
Symptom. While evaluating another pattern, the Gatus availability probe was recreated without its configuration, without its volumes and with the default service account, while ArgoCD showed it as Healthy and Synced throughout.

Cause. The same transition window: the old definition read a restructured values file and no longer recognized anything in it. A render with default values is a valid render, so no error.

Fix. Rolled back in about a minute.

Lesson. Judge a migration on pod creation time, never on Healthy / Synced alone.

docs.title: The control plane saturated with no memory alert
docs.text:
Symptom. At cluster startup, the Gateway became unreachable, and the controller-manager, the scheduler and the GitOps controllers restarted in a chain.

Cause. On a 2 vCPU server, the GitOps cascade pushed control plane CPU to 132%. Health probes timed out. No classic memory signal fired.

Fix. Move to 4 vCPU (cx33): 28% CPU, no more restarts, +€3.60/month.

Lesson. Size for the startup peak, and watch control plane CPU before memory. → Decision 002

docs.title: An "impossible" bug, tracked down to its real cause
docs.text:
Symptom. Subprocesses read null bytes instead of their output: ArgoCD (git fetch), PostgreSQL backups, Velero.

Cause. The OBI eBPF instrumentation, which places probes inside processes. I proved it with an A/B test on PostgreSQL: excluding the pod from instrumentation was enough to restore backups. The symptom first pointed to ArgoCD, the Talos kernel or the CloudNativePG plugin.

Fix. Remove OBI, instrument with the OpenTelemetry SDK instead.

Lesson. A component that modifies other processes is suspect by default, and every suspicion is tested with an A/B before acting. → Decisions 005 and 011

docs.title: The managed control plane that was too slow
docs.text:
Symptom. On Scaleway Kapsule, GitOps converged poorly on a cluster of only 56 pods.

Cause. 0.73 s per etcd request on the free shared control plane. This limit appears nowhere in the documentation.

Lesson. Measure etcd_request_duration_seconds before migrating, not after. → Decision 004

docs.title: ArgoCD cut itself off from the API
docs.text:
Symptom. At startup, ArgoCD stopped applying anything, and everything that talks to the Kubernetes API went down with it.

Cause. Within the same wave, ArgoCD applies resources in alphabetical order. A network allow policy came before the default-deny policy that contained the API access. ArgoCD lost the API before it could apply the rule that gave it back.

Fix. The default-deny policy is applied in the very first wave.

Lesson. Flux applied everything in a single pass and hid the flaw. Changing tools reveals implicit dependencies.

docs.title: Intermittent 404s on ArgoCD
docs.text:
Cause. Under a wildcard certificate, HTTP/2 reuses an open connection for another host (connection coalescing). Requests landed on a TLS chain that had no route to ArgoCD.

Fix. ArgoCD went back to standard TLS termination, which a recent Cilium option made possible.

docs.title: Velero backups rejected by Backblaze B2
docs.text:
Cause. Velero's AWS plugin always sends a tagging header that B2 rejects. The header is signed: it cannot be removed downstream without breaking the signature.

Fix. A signing proxy that strips the header and re-signs the request. The upstream fix is merged but not yet released. The exit condition is written down: remove the proxy as soon as a release contains it.

Lesson. Every workaround is logged in a register with its upstream cause, its link and its exit condition. Without an exit condition, a workaround is not documented, it is buried.

docs.title: Other workarounds kept up to date
docs.text: Component Problem Workaround Authentik The default shared memory (64 Mi) saturates, causing 502s 256 Mi memory volume mounted on /dev/shm Backstage OIDC discovery is only attempted at startup, with no retry An init container waits for Authentik to respond n8n OIDC SSO is reserved for the Enterprise edition OIDC routes added through the supported external hooks Gatus The configuration written by the sidecar is only read on the second start Restart at boot kept, upstream fix tracked Let's Encrypt Quota of 5 certificates per week, exhausted by rebuilds Certificates backed up before destruction, reinjected on rebuild

docs.title: Accepted limits and next steps
docs.text: What the platform does not do, or does not do yet. Most are costed choices; the rest form the roadmap.

docs.title: Deliberate choices
docs.text: Limit Why it is acceptable here What would lift it No high availability, a single etcd member Single-user service; rebuild and backups tested (003) Third-party users or an availability commitment Kyverno best practices in audit, not enforcement A single person deploys (010) A second team on the cluster No permanent staging environment The 24/7 cost of a second environment; a local Kind cluster replays the full GitOps chain to test Backstage Several contributors, or risky production releases Dependence on SaaS (Infisical, Cloudflare, Backblaze B2, GitHub) Nothing to operate, free tiers are enough A sovereignty or network isolation requirement Terraform CI runs plan only, triggered manually The admin API is filtered to the administrator's IP: a CI runner would always show up as drift A list of static allowed IPs Default alert rules follow their upstream repo Freezing them would mean copying the chart's list, which would drift in turn An upstream-modified alert threshold that causes problems

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
• SRE agent (in development). It runs in manual mode: it investigates, notifies and proposes pull requests, and a human decides. Before considering an automatic mode: tool-by-tool least-privilege hardening, and a global LLM consumption budget.
  • Lint in CI for Backstage. Run locally before every push; the CI job is ready, to be enabled as soon as a second contributor arrives.
  • Move the PostgreSQL backup plugin to its official Helm chart, now available.

docs.title: What I would do with a team
docs.text:
• Switch the Kyverno policies to enforcement, rule by rule, with a prior audit period.
  • Add a pre-production environment and an explicit promotion between environments.
  • Put access to the SRE agent behind a per-user identity (OAuth) rather than a shared token.
  • Federate LLM calls behind a gateway (budgets, provider failover) as soon as a second consumer exists.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
Every page follows the same outline: context → decision → rejected alternatives → trade-offs and cost → when to revisit. Trade-offs are spelled out in black and white: a choice with no cost is not a choice.

# Decision The trade-off accepted 001 Talos Linux on Hetzner, provisioned by a maintained Terraform module Depending on the module's defaults, partly unusable as is 002 A single control plane, cx33 minimum No fault tolerance on etcd: losing the node forces a rebuild 003 No high availability: self-healing rather than continuity Every component is a single point of failure, by choice 004 Hetzner → Infomaniak → Scaleway → Hetzner Three provider switches, absorbed by IaC and GitOps 005 ArgoCD → Flux → ArgoCD Flux has the better architecture, ArgoCD dominates the market: I chose the market 006 App-of-apps discovered by folder, ordered by waves A serialized cold start, slower 007 A home-grown App / Database API with Crossplane One more abstraction layer to maintain and test 008 Gateway API served by Cilium, with no separate ingress controller Coupling to the CNI, to be paid again when moving to managed Kubernetes 009 Secrets in Infisical, synced by External Secrets Depending on a SaaS to start the cluster 010 Kyverno: audit for best practices, enforcement for data Best-practice violations are reported, not prevented 011 Remove eBPF instrumentation in favor of the OpenTelemetry SDK Changing application code in order to trace it 012 No Rendered Manifests Pattern, a render diff in CI instead No Git history of rendered manifests

docs.title: Evaluated and rejected
docs.text:
A short list of tools evaluated then declined, with the reason in one line:

Tool Why not Terragrunt A single cluster, no multi-environment need Kargo, promotion through environment folders No persistent environment to promote to: a permanent staging would cost 24/7 for a single person Per-PR preview environments Full plan costed (~+€15/month, 17 files across 3 repos), dropped: GitOps adds latency where ephemeral should be disposable vCluster Crossplane is cluster-wide: everything would have to be recreated in each vCluster ARM (cax31) More expensive per GB of RAM (€1.57 vs €1.27) and application images are amd64 only Backup encryption (AGE) Bucket already private; key management costs more than the risk covered Self-hosted Infisical The free tier covers the need with nothing to operate kagent, LiteLLM, agentgateway A shared gateway only pays off from two consumers; there is only one Read-only "everything except Secrets" for Backstage Impossible in Kubernetes RBAC: a * rule includes Secrets, and no webhook filters reads

docs.title: 001 · Talos Linux on Hetzner, provisioned by a maintained Terraform module
docs.text:
In one sentence: I use a maintained community Terraform module rather than writing or forking my own provisioning, and I only override what is broken.

Status Date Repo Adopted 2026-02, renewed in 2026-09 talos-infra

docs.title: Context
docs.text: I need a reproducible Kubernetes cluster that I can destroy in the evening and recreate the next day to control cost. Kubernetes "by hand" on VMs means managing the OS, updates, SSH and hardening.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Talos Linux as the OS: immutable, no SSH or shell, fully driven by API. There is nothing to patch by hand, and the attack surface is minimal.
  • Terraform module hcloud-k8s/kubernetes/hcloud (pinned version): it installs Talos, Cilium, the Hetzner integrations (load balancer, encrypted volumes) and etcd backup.
  • Principles set from the first PRD (design document): no Terragrunt, no fork, no SOPS.

docs.title: Alternatives rejected
docs.text: Alternative Why not Write my own Terraform resources Reinventing what a maintained module already does, and maintaining it alone Fork the module Losing upstream updates; every bump becomes a manual merge Managed Kubernetes Tried twice (Infomaniak, Scaleway), see decision 004

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text: Not all of the module's defaults were usable. The image builder's server type (cpx11) could no longer be ordered in Europe, and the default Talos version was newer than the available talosctl client. Both are overridden explicitly, with the reason in a comment.

docs.title: When to revisit
docs.text: If the module is no longer maintained, or if a multi-cluster need appears (Terragrunt would become relevant again).

docs.title: 002 · A single control plane, cx33 minimum
docs.text:
In one sentence: one control plane instead of three divides the cost of the most expensive line item, and the daily etcd backup covers the real recovery need.

Status Date Repo Adopted 2026-09 talos-infra

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A highly available control plane needs three nodes (etcd needs a majority). The cluster is single-user, and it is regularly destroyed and recreated.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• A single control plane, dedicated to Kubernetes: it refuses applications (NoSchedule taint). Two workers carry the load.
  • Floor size cx33 (4 vCPU / 8 GB), set by measurement.

docs.title: The measurement that set the size
docs.text:
On a cx23 (2 vCPU), the initial GitOps sync saturated the control plane at 132% CPU. No memory alert fired: no OOMKilled, no MemoryPressure. The real symptom was a cascade of restarts (controller-manager, scheduler, GitOps controllers) caused by health probe timeouts.

After moving to cx33: 28% CPU, no more restarts. The resize was done in place in 1 min 9 s, with no etcd loss. Cost of the upgrade: +€3.60/month.

Lesson: on a control plane, the bottleneck is CPU at startup, not memory in steady state. Size for the peak of the cascade, not for idle.

docs.title: Alternatives rejected
docs.text: Alternative Why not 3 control planes ×3 on the most expensive line item, for a service with no third-party users Control planes that also carry applications That was the old topology: applications competed with etcd and the API

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text:
etcd has a single member: no fault tolerance. Losing the node forces a rebuild of the cluster, not an in-place repair. The daily etcd snapshot to Backblaze B2 (outside Hetzner) and the rebuild through Terraform + GitOps make this risk acceptable.

The resize is also irreversible: Hetzner can grow the disk but cannot shrink it.

docs.title: When to revisit
docs.text: As soon as the cluster carries a service with third-party users, or an availability commitment.

docs.title: 003 · No high availability: self-healing rather than continuity
docs.text:
In one sentence: every component is a single point of failure, by a written and costed economic choice; the platform can repair and rebuild itself, but not stay up during an outage.

Status Date Repo Adopted 2026-09 talos-infra, talos-argocd

docs.title: Context
docs.text: High availability is not a setting, it is a sum of costs. The service has one user, and downtime has no business cost.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
No continuity mechanism: one replica per application, one PostgreSQL instance, no PodDisruptionBudget, no autoscaling, a single zone.

What is covered instead:

  • ArgoCD reconciles every 1 to 2 minutes: any change made outside Git is reverted.
  • ExternalDNS rewires DNS to the new IP by itself after a full rebuild.
  • External Secrets + Reloader: rotating a secret restarts the affected pods with no intervention.
  • Gatus and Slack alerts to detect, B2 backups to restore.

docs.title: What each lever would have cost
docs.text: Lever Cost Several replicas ~+0.5 Gi of reserved RAM per replica and per application PostgreSQL with 2 instances One more pod, doubled storage PodDisruptionBudget Free, but useless without replicas; it would even block node maintenance Autoscaling (HPA) Assumes capacity that is paid for and permanently unused HA control plane ×3 on the most expensive line item Multi-zone Duplicated workers, cross-zone traffic, volumes that cannot be attached across zones

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text: A node loss or an update causes an interruption, limited to the time pods take to restart elsewhere.

docs.title: When to revisit
docs.text: As soon as a service has third-party users or an availability commitment is made.

docs.title: 004 · Hetzner → Infomaniak → Scaleway → Hetzner
docs.text:
In one sentence: I left Hetzner for managed Kubernetes to cut cost and eliminate a bug, then came back because the free managed offerings gave out on control plane reliability.

Status Date Repo Adopted: Hetzner, separate control plane and workers 2026-02 → 2026-09-12 talos-infra

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text: When Where Why we leave / arrive 2026-02 Hetzner + Talos, 3 control planes that also carry applications Starting point 2026-07 Infomaniak KaaS (managed) The managed control plane is free, so real workers for the same budget; and a corrupted-pipe bug seemed to come from Talos (~€33-38/month at Hetzner at the time) 2026-09 Scaleway Kapsule (managed), attempt The Infomaniak API timed out very often, while the cluster is recreated frequently 2026-09-12 Back to Hetzner, 1 control plane + 2 workers Scaleway ruled out in a day: 0.73 s per etcd request on the shared control plane, with only 56 pods. The cx33 type was available again at Hetzner

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Back to self-managed on Hetzner, this time with a dedicated control plane and two workers. I keep control of the OS and the network (Cilium with Gateway API, which a managed offering did not let me configure fully).

docs.title: What these migrations taught me
docs.text:
• On a managed control plane, measure etcd latency before migrating the GitOps. The advertised limits (RAM, node count) were never reached: it was the undocumented latency that gave out.
  • Server type availability changes without notice. At Hetzner, cx43/cx53 disappeared and cx33 went through three states in an hour. Availability is checked at every apply.
  • The "Talos bug" was not one. It came from the eBPF instrumentation, which I eventually isolated with an A/B (see decision 011).

docs.title: Rejected alternatives
docs.text: Alternative Why not Stay on Infomaniak Recurring API timeouts, incompatible with a frequently recreated cluster Scaleway Kapsule etcd latency of the shared control plane; Cilium's Gateway API cannot be enabled (operator configuration out of reach) ARM at Hetzner (cax31) More expensive per GB of RAM, and applications published for amd64 only

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text: Three switches in two months, each run as a project: PRD, milestones, closing measurement. It is also the best proof of the platform's portability: Terraform + GitOps rebuilt it identically on three providers. Current cost: €41.36/month.

docs.title: 005 · ArgoCD → Flux → ArgoCD
docs.text:
In one sentence: I tested Flux in real conditions for four months. Its architecture is better, but ArgoCD is the market standard, and the outage that had pushed me to leave turned out to be unrelated to ArgoCD: I switched back.

Status Date Repo Adopted: ArgoCD Flux on 2026-05-30, back to ArgoCD on 2026-09-13 talos-argocd (formerly talos-fluxcd)

docs.title: Why I tested Flux
docs.text:
Two reasons, arriving at the same time:

  1. The release of the Flux Operator Web UI. The lack of a UI was the main criticism of Flux against ArgoCD. A built-in UI, with OIDC SSO and a delivery pipeline graph, removed that argument. It was the time to compare the two tools on a real cluster.
  2. A recurring outage on the ArgoCD side. The component that reads Git (repo-server) failed at cluster startup (git fetch exit 128). A Flux PoC on the same cluster gave 0 errors, against 16 on the ArgoCD side.

docs.title: What four months of Flux taught me
docs.text:
Flux has the better architecture. Specialized controllers (sources, Kustomize, Helm) rather than a central server. Native dependencies between components (dependsOn + wait), CEL health checks, and the application of a component in a single pass.

But it is harder to pick up. There are more objects to understand, state is spread across several controllers, and debugging goes through the CLI more than through an overview.

docs.title: Why I went back to ArgoCD
docs.text:
1. The market. ArgoCD is the most requested GitOps engine in platform teams. Mastering it in depth (ordering, Application health, render diff in CI) is worth more for my engagements.
  2. The outage was not ArgoCD's. The same signature (null bytes in a subprocess's output) appeared on other components. I isolated it with an A/B: it came from the OBI eBPF instrumentation (decision 011). Before switching back, I ran another proof on a dedicated bench: 334 instrumented git fetch, 0 errors. Then, in production, 0 occurrences over more than 40,000 log lines, across five full startups.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Back to ArgoCD. This is not a revert: the repo was rewritten, and it takes over what Flux did better. Startup ordering becomes explicit (decision 006), and health checks written in Lua replace Flux's CEL ones.

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text:
• ArgoCD has no dependsOn between Applications: it took waves and a Lua health check.
  • Two complete GitOps migrations. Both were absorbed without touching the applications.

docs.title: What I take from it
docs.text:
• Comparing two tools on a real cluster teaches more than a feature matrix.
  • A component that instruments other processes is a default suspect in any "impossible" diagnosis. Every suspicion is verified with an A/B before acting.

docs.title: 006 · App-of-apps discovered by folder, ordered by waves
docs.text:
In one sentence: adding a component means dropping a file in a folder, and startup order is guaranteed by waves that wait for the previous wave to be healthy.

Status Date Repo Adopted 2026-09 talos-argocd

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A platform has strict dependencies: an operator's types (CRDs) must exist before the resources that use them, and a certificate needs the Cloudflare secret, itself provided by External Secrets. During the first pass on ArgoCD, 26 syncs launched at the same time had brought a cluster to its knees.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• A root Application recursively discovers every application.yaml. No central registry.
  • Waves (sync-wave): wave N+1 only starts once wave N is synced and healthy. ArgoCD disabled child Application health by default: I restore it with a Lua script, without which the waves wait for nothing.
  • The root manages itself: it is one of its own sources.
  • A single convention: <category>/<component>/application.yaml + values.yaml + resources/. No exceptions, no umbrella folder.

docs.title: Rejected alternatives
docs.text: Alternative Why not ApplicationSets More concurrency on Git operations (a factor in the bug of decision 005), and more indirect to read Progressive Syncs (RollingSync) Feature still behind a flag, and it disables auto-sync on the generated Applications: we would lose self-healing Kustomize Removed: every file was declared two or three times (the file, the folder index, the parent index)

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text:
• Cold start is serialized, so slower than a parallel start, but it converges on its own (33/33 Applications at the last full startup).
  • Automatic discovery has a downside: a path error can trigger a deletion (prune). This is contained at three levels: a CI check on every Application, a Kyverno policy that blocks the deletion of resources carrying data, and continuous backups (incident under control).

docs.title: 007 · A homemade App / Database API with Crossplane
docs.text:
In one sentence: a developer describes their application in 15 lines; the platform generates the accompanying Kubernetes resources and applies best practices on their behalf.

Status Date Repo Adopted 2026-03 talos-argocd

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Deploying an application properly on this platform takes about ten objects: Deployment, Service, HTTPS route, HTTP redirect, network policy, registry pull secrets, monitoring. Writing them by hand for each application means copying mistakes.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Two homemade types exposed by Crossplane v2:

apiVersion: taloslab.cc/v1alpha1
kind: App
metadata:
  name: saveit
spec:
  image: ghcr.io/…/saveit:0.2.11
  hostname: saveit.taloslab.cc
  size: medium          # small | medium | large → requests / limits
  migrate: true         # database migrations before startup (initContainer)
  workerCommand: "…"    # second Deployment for background jobs
  metrics: true         # ServiceMonitor + dashboard
The developer writes The platform generates kind: App ServiceAccount, Deployment (+ worker), Service, 2 HTTPRoutes (HTTPS + redirect), CiliumNetworkPolicy, ExternalSecrets, ConfigMap, ServiceMonitor kind: Database CloudNativePG PostgreSQL cluster, PodMonitor, scheduled backup and continuous archiving to B2
  • The composition logic is written in Python (function-pythonic): readable, testable, rendered outside the cluster by crossplane render.
  • End-to-end Chainsaw tests on an ephemeral Kind cluster in CI, plus a check that the generated code is up to date.
  • Each resource's status is surfaced in Backstage with readable conditions.

docs.title: Alternatives rejected
docs.text: Alternative Why not A shared Helm chart No status or continuous reconciliation; each team can override anything Pure YAML compositions (patch & transform) Unreadable as soon as there are conditions Crossplane Operations (alpha), Usage / deletion protection Excessive for two applications; a Kyverno policy does the same job more simply Crossplane multi-team RBAC Designed for several teams, pointless for one person

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text: One more layer to maintain. Defaults live in the API definition (XRD) and only apply at admission, so test examples must write them explicitly. Changing a field's type requires a migration procedure.

docs.title: 008 · Gateway API served by Cilium, with no separate ingress controller
docs.text:
In one sentence: Cilium already does networking and policies; giving it HTTP ingress too removes one component to operate, at the price of a deliberate coupling.

Status Date Repo Adopted 2026-09 talos-infra, talos-argocd

docs.title: Context
docs.text: I need an HTTPS entry point for public services. The legacy Ingress is replaced by the Gateway API, the current Kubernetes standard. During the Infomaniak stint, I used Envoy Gateway.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Cilium serves the Gateway API, replacing kube-proxy, with the Hetzner load balancer driven by annotations.
  • A generic HTTPS listener on the wildcard certificate: a new application is reachable without changing the Gateway.
  • ArgoCD is exposed like the other services (TLS termination), no longer in passthrough.

docs.title: Alternatives rejected
docs.text: Alternative Why not Envoy Gateway / ingress-nginx One more component to operate and update TLS passthrough for ArgoCD Under a wildcard certificate, HTTP/2 reuses another host's connection (connection coalescing, RFC 7540): intermittent 404s. Cilium 1.20 allows disabling the gRPC-web translation that forced passthrough One certificate per host Let's Encrypt quota (5 per week), and a file to edit for every new host

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text: Coupling to the CNI. Moving to a managed Kubernetes, where the CNI is not mine, will require reintroducing an ingress controller. That is precisely what blocked on Scaleway (decision 004).

docs.title: 009 · Secrets in Infisical, synced by External Secrets
docs.text:
In one sentence: no secret in Git or in the Terraform state; the cluster fetches its secrets from an external vault and restarts pods when they change.

Status Date Repo Adopted 2026-02 talos-infra, talos-argocd

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Infisical (SaaS, EU region) is the vault. External Secrets Operator creates the Kubernetes secrets from the vault. Reloader restarts pods when a secret changes.
  • Terraform deposits only one bootstrap secret (the Infisical machine identity), via write-only attributes: the value never ends up in the Terraform state.
  • Crossplane compositions create an application's ExternalSecrets themselves.

docs.title: Alternatives rejected
docs.text: Alternative Why not SOPS / Sealed Secrets Encrypted secrets in Git stay in the history, and key rotation is manual Self-hosted Infisical One more critical service to operate and back up; the free tier is enough Vault / OpenBao Oversized for one person

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text: Cluster startup depends on an external SaaS: if Infisical is unavailable, new secrets are not created (those already present stay in place).

docs.title: 010 · Kyverno: audit for best practices, blocking for data
docs.text:
In one sentence: best-practice rules flag without blocking, because there is only one user; the only blocking rule protects what is unrecoverable, the data.

Status Date Repo Adopted 2026-04 talos-argocd

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Policy Mode Why Unprivileged containers, non-root, no host namespaces, with requests / limits, allowed registries Audit Visibility is enough for a single user; blocking makes sense when several teams deploy Validation of App / Database claims, uniqueness of hostnames Audit Same reason Deletion of a Crossplane resource without the allow-delete annotation Blocking A database deleted by mistake cannot be rebuilt from Git

The policies are written in CEL (Kubernetes' native expression language), the old ClusterPolicy format being phased out.

docs.title: What the blocking rule has already prevented
docs.text: During the incident of 2026-09-15, this policy refused the deletion of the Crossplane resources and stopped the cascade.

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text: Bad practices are visible in reports, not prevented. A non-compliant deployment goes through.

docs.title: When to revisit
docs.text: As soon as a second person or team deploys on the cluster: switch to blocking, rule by rule.

docs.title: 011 · Remove eBPF instrumentation in favor of the OpenTelemetry SDK
docs.text:
In one sentence: "no code change" eBPF instrumentation turned out to be intrusive; for an application whose code I control, the OpenTelemetry SDK does better, with no privileges.

Status Date Repo Adopted 2026-09-12 talos-argocd, saveit application

docs.title: Context
docs.text: OBI (OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation) traces applications without modifying their images: a privileged DaemonSet places probes inside processes. Adopted in February 2026, it initially covered all namespaces.

docs.title: What I measured
docs.text:
• The eBPF probes disrupted pipe reads in the instrumented processes. I proved it with an A/B on the PostgreSQL backups: excluding the pod from instrumentation was enough to restore them.
  • The symptom looked like bugs in other components (ArgoCD, Talos kernel, CloudNativePG plugin): a privileged DaemonSet writing into process memory clouds every diagnosis.
  • About 350 Mi of memory per node to trace a single Django application.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Remove OBI, instrument the application with the OpenTelemetry SDK: ORM, HTTP and worker spans, and a trace_id in every log emitted under a span. Traces go to VictoriaTraces, metrics to VictoriaMetrics.

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text: Code has to be modified to trace. The "zero modification" argument only holds for third-party applications, and there are none here.

docs.title: What I take from it
docs.text: Before removing OBI, every suspicion was tested with an A/B: one proven (PostgreSQL), two not reproduced (ArgoCD, Authentik). An 863-line workaround put in place for Authentik turned out to be unnecessary and was removed, with evidence.

docs.title: 012 · No Rendered Manifests Pattern, a render diff in CI instead
docs.text:
In one sentence: committing rendered manifests cost more than it brought at this scale; a render diff posted as a comment on each PR gives the same review without the artifact.

Status Date Repo Rejected twice, definitively on 2026-09-15 talos-argocd

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Rendered Manifests Pattern consists of committing the final rendered YAML (Helm, Kustomize) so that Git shows exactly what is running. The pattern is highly recommended in the GitOps literature.

docs.title: Why not
docs.text:
1. ArgoCD's native implementation (Source Hydrator) cannot express this repo: 23 Applications out of 37 combine a remote chart, values and local manifests. Both gaps are open upstream requests.
  2. Rendering in CI does not faithfully reproduce the cluster: 17 charts out of 22 read the real API capabilities (.Capabilities), which a CI does not know, and 7 emit Helm hooks that the pattern loses.
  3. The migration opens a risk window per component. During the trial, a component was rendered with its default values while still showing Healthy. Spotted and rolled back in a minute (see incidents).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: argocd-diff-preview in CI: each PR receives as a comment the diff of the manifests rendered on both sides. It is the same information for review, with no artifact to maintain.

docs.title: Trade-offs and cost
docs.text: No Git history of rendered manifests: no git blame on a final object.

docs.title: When to revisit
docs.text: If the history of rendered manifests is ever needed to track down a regression, if a cold start fails for lack of access to chart repos, or if the upstream requests ship.

docs.title: sre-agent: the LLM-driven SRE agent
docs.text:
A Kubernetes controller detects a failure, an LLM agent investigates with read-only tools, then proposes a fix, through a pull request when the resource is managed by GitOps.

Role Automatic failure diagnosis, remediation under human control Status In development, deployed in manual mode Tools TypeScript (MCP server, Vercel AI SDK), Go (kubebuilder controller), Helm, VictoriaMetrics MCP Visibility Private

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant K as Cluster (Events)
    participant C as Go controller
    participant A as Agent (MCP server)
    participant O as Metrics / Logs / Traces
    participant S as Slack / GitHub
    K->>C: Event (e.g. CrashLoopBackOff)
    C->>C: 4 filters: repetition, rate,<br/>cool-down, still failing?
    C->>A: Investigation request
    A->>K: kubectl get / describe / logs (read)
    A->>O: Observability queries
    A->>A: Analysis, fix validated with a dry-run
    A->>S: Report + proposed options<br/>or GitOps pull request

docs.title: Notable choices
docs.text: Choice Reason Manual mode in production: the agent notifies and proposes, a human decides An LLM makes mistakes; trust is built before automation GitOps-managed resource → pull request, never kubectl A direct fix would be reverted by ArgoCD and create drift Four filters on the controller side before calling the LLM A flapping failure should not trigger an investigation on every event Fix validated server-side with a dry-run (--dry-run=server) before being proposed Only propose what the Kubernetes API would accept VictoriaMetrics' official MCP servers rather than rewriting tools Less code; the agent is an MCP client of observability Several LLM providers behind a single model table Being able to switch models without touching code Shared token rather than OAuth A single user, service internal to the cluster

docs.title: Where it comes from
docs.text: The project carries a slice of an existing open source project (dot-ai). A first attempt had diverged too far from upstream and was abandoned. Lesson: re-read the upstream code at every decision. About 170 tests (Vitest on the TypeScript side, Ginkgo / envtest on the Go side).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Tool-by-tool least-privilege hardening and a global LLM consumption budget, before any automatic mode. See the roadmap.

docs.title: talos-argocd: the GitOps repo
docs.text:
The desired state of the whole cluster: 35 infrastructure components, the business applications and the Crossplane self-service API.

Role Source of truth for what runs in the cluster Tools ArgoCD, Helm, Crossplane v2 (Python compositions), Kyverno, Cilium, Chainsaw Visibility Private

docs.title: What it contains
docs.text:
• infrastructure/: the components, sorted by category (controllers, configs, observability, platform). Each follows the same convention: application.yaml + values.yaml + resources/.
  • apps/prod/: the business applications, each described by a 15-line App claim.
  • crossplane/: the compositions' Python code, the examples and the Chainsaw tests.
  • clusters/dev/: the subset replayed on Backstage's local Kind cluster.

docs.title: CI on every pull request
docs.text: Check What it guarantees Application validation Each Git source explicitly declares its read mode, and no Kustomize file comes back (a guardrail born from the incident) CRD consistency Test versions match the production ones kube-linter, Trivy Best practices and configuration argocd-diff-preview The diff of rendered manifests is posted as a PR comment, deletions included Crossplane Lint, generated code up to date, render outside the cluster, then 6 end-to-end tests on Kind

docs.title: In numbers
docs.text: 35 infrastructure Applications, 19 synced secrets, 13 Cilium network policies, 11 Kyverno policies, 2 homemade APIs, about 950 commits. Renovate proposes updates with a maturity delay: 3 days for a patch, 7 for a minor or major version.

docs.title: talos-backstage: the developer portal
docs.text:
A Backstage form becomes a GitOps pull request: a repo, an application or a database in self-service, with SSO and an MCP server to drive the portal from an AI assistant.

Role Self-service interface on top of the Crossplane API Tools Backstage (new plugin system), TypeScript, Authentik OIDC, PostgreSQL, Kind Visibility Private

docs.title: What a developer sees
docs.text:
• Create a repo from a Python/Flask or Go skeleton, with CI and Dockerfile ready.
  • Create an application or a database. The forms are generated automatically from the Crossplane APIs: adding a field to the API adds it to the form.
  • Modify or delete a component, always by pull request.
  • See the real state: ArgoCD sync, pods, Kyverno policies, Crossplane resources, Grafana dashboards, DORA metrics.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
• A scaffolder module with three homemade actions and a processor that cleans the generated forms: it removes technical settings and carries over the API's required fields.
  • A plugin published on npm that syncs Authentik users and groups into the catalog (open source).
  • A faithful local environment: a Kind cluster with Cilium and Gateway API, which replays the full GitOps chain to test a form end to end.

docs.title: Notable choices
docs.text: Choice Reason Plugins declared explicitly Automatic loading does not pick up frontend plugins in the version used ArgoCD plugin pinned, excluded from Renovate Later versions require a newer Backstage and would duplicate the framework's packages. The exit condition is written down Runtime image not distroless TechDocs generates the documentation in the container (Python + MkDocs); Alpine is incompatible with a native module Blocking vulnerability scan before publishing The only quality check run in CI: the image build is the job that counts PostgreSQL without backup in production All the portal's state can be rebuilt from GitHub and Authentik's configuration Kubernetes read access through an aggregated role, no * A * rule also gives access to Secrets

docs.title: talos-fluxcd: the Flux episode (archived)
docs.text:
The cluster's GitOps repo from May to September 2026, under Flux. Archived on the return to ArgoCD.

Period 2026-05-30 → 2026-09-13 Tools Flux (HelmRelease, Kustomization), Crossplane Visibility Private, archived

docs.title: Why it existed
docs.text: To compare Flux and ArgoCD on a real cluster, just as the Flux Operator Web UI removed the main criticism of Flux, the lack of a UI. A recurring outage on the ArgoCD side sped up the move. The whole story is in decision 005.

docs.title: What Flux did better, and had to be rebuilt under ArgoCD
docs.text: Under Flux Equivalent put in place under ArgoCD dependsOn + wait between components Ordered waves + Lua health check (006) CEL health checks Lua health scripts for Crossplane resources Application in a single pass Explicit order, which revealed a hidden dependency between network policies (incident)

docs.title: What I take from it
docs.text: Flux has the better architecture, but it is more demanding to pick up. ArgoCD remains the market standard, hence the return. And the outage followed the cluster under Flux, which made it possible to find its real cause, unrelated to either tool.

docs.title: talos-infra: the infrastructure
docs.text:
One task apply creates the servers, installs the OS and Kubernetes, then hands over to ArgoCD.

Role Provision the cluster and bootstrap it into GitOps Tools Terraform, hcloud-k8s module, Talos Linux, Cilium, Taskfile, Devbox Visibility Private

docs.title: What it contains
docs.text:
• Terraform: Hetzner servers (1 control plane + 2 workers), network, firewall, load balancer, installation of ArgoCD and the root Application. The Terraform state is stored outside Hetzner (Backblaze B2).
  • The full lifecycle as tasks: apply (creation + convergence), destroy (clean teardown, DNS neutralized), PostgreSQL restore, TLS quota check, tests of the network and Kyverno policies.
  • The operations runbooks: disaster recovery, backup and restore, adding a component or a route, network policies, sizing.
  • The PRDs: nearly 50 closed design documents, with their decisions, milestones and measured results.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The cluster is disposable. It is destroyed and recreated regularly to control cost. Everything that must survive (Terraform state, etcd snapshots, PostgreSQL logs, Velero backups) lives on Backblaze B2.
  • No secret in the Terraform state thanks to write-only attributes.
  • Terraform bootstraps ArgoCD then lets go: ArgoCD then manages itself from Git, with no ownership conflict with Terraform.
  • A register of workarounds, each with its upstream cause and exit condition, re-read at every update of the component concerned.

docs.title: talos-landing: the showcase
docs.text:
A public page that displays the real state of the cluster (nodes, load, components, services), read directly from the Kubernetes API every 30 seconds.

Role Cluster showcase, public entry point Tools Flask, HTMX, AlpineJS, Tailwind CSS, Python Kubernetes client Visibility Public: github.com/naqa92-portfolio-projects/talos-landing

docs.title: Notable choices
docs.text: Choice Reason Server-side rendering + HTMX refresh No JavaScript framework for a status page Visible services are declared by annotation on their route Exposing a service on the showcase requires no change to the showcase Explicit demo mode (TALOS_MOCK=1) An implicit demo mode would pass a broken service account off as a healthy cluster Controlled degradation If the API or a CRD is missing, the page still renders with the "unknown" state Non-root image, blocking vulnerability scan The pipeline builds, scans, publishes, then opens the update PR in the GitOps repo
